There are two types of virtualization possible today, separated into two types, based on how they work:

* Type 1 Hypervisor - software virtualization, runs as a program from within another operating system. Has very significant performance impacts and generally less customization.
* Type 2 Hypervisor - a super slimmed down operating system made just for virtualization is either laid down on the hardware from the date the system is set up, or shimmed in between the previous operating system and bare metal later.

A well-known virtualization platform is a type 2 hypervisor. It's the free and impressive virtualization platform made by a large tech company, and built in (but not enabled by default) on newer versions of their operating system.

What you can do from newer versions of the operating system is use your PC, get it configured the way you want to as your daily driver machine. When you're ready, add the feature for the virtualization platform. Now, some low-level things happen. The virtualization platform is turned on, and transparently becomes the actual operating system running on your hardware (the 'bare metal' hypervisor, it is called).

Your host operating system, the one you were running pre-virtualization, becomes a special type of deified virtual machine called the host partition, which is basically a virtual machine that is able to see the physical devices on your computer. The cool thing about it is that you still log on to your host operating system when you use the system; you just access child virtual machines using the virtualization application. Super cool, it's how myself and my colleagues do use-case testing for our clients all day, every day.

Any future virtual machines created on the system are sometimes referred to as child partitions, and they can only see a subset of virtual references to these hardware devices. There do exist technologies to map a GPU through the bare metal to a child virtual machine, for instance. Another common use case is to map certain hard drives or arrays of drives through to child virtual machines, commonly called pass-through disks.

You'll find that people readily attempt to hack out of the virtual machine sandbox to touch the host operating system, but virtualization by its very nature with type 2 hypervisors almost inhibits it from the get-go. Type 1 hypervisors are much, much more susceptible to the sorts of attacks you suggest.

A cloud service provider is a great example. It's easy to configure an application with a load balancer. We can use the load balancer to gauge how many users are trying to access our site at a given time. If traffic exceeds the capacity of one host, we can instruct our web service to add another host to share the load.

These new workers are just here to help us with traffic and keep our application responsive and fast. They will probably be instructed to pull down the newest source code on first boot and be configured not to save any files locally. Instead, they'll likely get a shared drive, pooled among all of the other workers.

Since they're not saving files locally, we really don't care about the host machine. As long as users have completed their session, it can be terminated at any point. This is what it means to be stateless.

The workers make their mark on the world by committing permanent changes to a database or shared drive.

So, new worker instances come online as needed. They don't need to be permanently online, though, and don't need to preserve their history, so in that sense, they are stateless. After the load drops, the unneeded little workers save their changes and then go to sleep until needed again in the future.

A virtual machine is about as sandboxed as you can get. You've got a hypervisor coordinating actual activities on the physical hardware, and your virtual machines queue up to run their commands (terrible and overly simplistic explanation warning). But in most conditions, nearly all, your virtual machines are not able to step into neighboring virtual machines' memory space, write over their files, or destroy their neighbors.

However, to do this you've got many copies of essentially the same thing. If you have five instances of an operating system which each service one application, you're essentially duplicating five full installs of that operating system, plus five copies of all of your program prerequisites. There could be hundreds of gigs of duplicated content there.

Now, when you containerize, rather than five instances of that operating system, you've got one, and each container is able to share prerequisites.

This is great because you're able to cram way more services and usefulness onto the same hardware than you could with virtual machines.

The key benefit of containerization is that it allows users to package an application with all of its dependencies into a standardized unit for software development.

I think this was a poorly worded line from the original post. Containerizing gives us all of those cool features I mentioned, but the really neat thing about this technology is that there is no install script.

When you're building an application and know you need certain prerequisites all set up just so, you as the developer set it up and get it working within the container. When you release to the wild, you use that same container. You get it working, put it in the container, and you know it will work with no problems on the receiving end.

Everything your application needs to run is bundled within the container, and you just hit start and voilà, out pops your application working with zero issues.

Again, containerization makes this easy. It's a lot harder when you have many applications on a system to get each of their permissions right. And what if all of them have common prerequisites? If you go overboard locking down the permissions, you suddenly are stuck duplicating copies of prerequisites (not fun) and you are doing a LOT of tweaking and hacking to make these things cohabitate.

This is all stuff that then becomes hard to automate and reproduce, taking us away from the model of automated deployments and reliability. Manual processes are super hard to get right consistently.

I would argue that while you definitely can do all of this without containerization, having it makes this a lot easier, for all of the reasons I mentioned here.
